children: By Chip Cutter and Ray A. Smith
The memo arrives in employees' inboxes with unsettling news but few specifics: Layoffs are coming. Soon.
Exactly who will get the ax, and when it will fall, isn't divulged. For staffers, it's too little information to plan around, and just enough to stoke weeks-even months-of worrying and guessing.

Call it the era of the looming layoff. At companies from Nike and Starbucks to Meta Platforms, a new playbook for cutting jobs is emerging, in which corporate bosses signal their intentions well in advance and fill in the details later.
The approach lets them telegraph to investors they're serious about "right-sizing," and to workers to get prepared. Back in the office, it's often a recipe for maximum anxiety.

Nike became the latest major company to pre-announce layoffs this way. The sportswear maker told staffers Thursday that it would shrink as part of an effort to speed up its operations-though not until 2027.

"This work will result in fewer roles across Nike," Chief Executive Elliott Hill wrote in a companywide memo. Nike's leadership wouldn't decide on which until next year. Any speculation meanwhile was premature, he added, "because we do not yet know the number of roles or specific locations of positions."

Other companies have taken a similar approach. Meta told employees in an internal memo in April that it would lay off 10% of its staff, or roughly 8,000 people, and that affected employees would learn their fate May 20. That gave staffers roughly a month to agonize over whether they would be on the list, some of them in public.

"Will I be affected? Will I be able to find another job as good as this one? Are my skills transferable? Will I have to take a step down?" one wrote on LinkedIn. Another, Robert Sweeney, who was an engineering manager at Meta, described the limbo period in the weeks before as a "death march" and said that colleagues furiously worked to finish deadlines in the hopes they would be spared.
"One, it was exhausting," said Sweeney, who resigned one day after the layoffs. "Two, as a manager, I had to pretend like everything was fine. Three, it felt exploitative to my team."

That's still better than ambushing workers all at once with mass layoffs, some executives say. At many companies, workers start whispering about possible cuts as soon as they spot leaders in impromptu huddles.

"People are not idiots," said Beth Steinberg, a veteran human-resources executive who has spent much of her career at technology companies. She argues it's usually best for bosses to share what they know when they know it, even if the information is frustratingly incomplete.
"Most companies don't want to be reckless about this decision, so it can take a long time to come to the conclusion of what needs to be eliminated and why," she said. "I prefer transparency."

Last year, Starbucks told employees in January that it would cut jobs by March. It didn't initially specify which roles would be impacted, only that in-store teams would be unaffected. A month later, the coffee giant began laying off 1,000 workers.

Likewise, Disney pre-announced 7,000 layoffs in 2023, which played out over multiple rounds. This year, layoffs have already hit divisions like marketing. Now it's planning a restructuring of its television operation that could result in hundreds of further cuts, The Wall Street Journal reported last week, citing people close to the matter. The plan might not be finalized before the end of the year, they said.

Just about every way of cutting jobs, of course, has trade-offs. Learning you have been laid off via text and email in the middle of the night-as some Amazon staffers did last year-isn't ideal. For employers, announcing a layoff months in advance also carries risks: The most in-demand employees could decide to end the uncertainty by jumping ship.

One reason executives say they wait to divulge layoff details is that many just don't know how big or small their companies should be in the future. Some large tech companies foresee a steady stream of cuts for years to come, while others say it's still unclear how artificial intelligence will affect head counts.
At Nike, the company acknowledged that the coming job reductions will create uncertainty.

"For most teammates, the work immediately in front of you remains the same," Hill, Nike's CEO, wrote in the memo. Those affected by layoffs will get clear timelines and support, he said, "as decisions are made."
